No viewing; based on published criticism and reference records. Status moved from HOLD to GREY (reservations). Rule 2 check: the film's Catholic content is the Gospel, not the post-conciliar Church, so it does not meet hard rule 2; the Nostra Aetate framing is treated as a reservation per the brief. Nostra Aetate link: Greydanus's review says the document 'might be' the main influence (his reading); his separate article states Zeffirelli 'has long cited' it. I found no primary Zeffirelli statement (autobiography or interview) and did not cite one. Paul VI (post-conciliar) mentioned for facts only, not as approval. Cut: recommend only the complete version (DFI 382 min; releases 365–386 min depending on PAL speed and edition). Avoid the 2000 Carlton 270-min abridgement and the shorter cinema cut. The words of institution at the Last Supper were not confirmed; the record now says only 'reverently staged'. The Danish Film Institute record is used as the identity source because no BFI page was found and Screenonline refused connection. The CBCEW/Peter Malone PDF previously cited could not be read (binary PDF) and has been dropped. Editor: if the Founder treats a rewritten Judas as grave enough to exclude, this would become REJECT on gravity, not on hard rule 2.

Research outcome was GREY; overruled by the editor: REJECT: Editor ruling under the Founder's position (2026-10-11). Zeffirelli shaped the film by Nostra Aetate, and that conciliar reading is built into the drama: the invented scribe Zerah engineers the arrest and Judas becomes a well-meaning dupe, shifting the Gospel account of responsibility. This is the post-conciliar outlook applied to the Gospel itself, not a reservation a viewer can set aside.

The film's seriousness, its martyrdom scenes and Kichijiro's repeated confessions are acknowledged; a viewer could weigh them only by setting aside the climax, which is the point of the film. the-agony-and-the-ecstasy.notes: Routes: AFI Catalog, DeSilva abstract (the PDF returned 403 by both WebFetch and direct request), and an English subtitle transcript: subtitlecat.com, 'The.Agony.and.the.Ecstasy.1965.1080p. Eng Sub-en.srt', saved in scratchpad\subs\the-agony-and-the-ecstasy\1\. Transcript: Julius defends the sword as necessary to keep the Church free (c. 00:29) and a cardinal later defends his policy (c. 02:03); Michelangelo calls Julius a 'freebooter' leading the Church (c. 00:38); 'it's a proof of faith... Not if you're a saint, or an artist. I am merely a pope' (c. 01:59); Julius says God sometimes seems deaf (c. 02:00) and that soon he will know whether the artist's conception of God is true (c. 02:12). The papacy is not caricatured and Julius is given dignity, so an editor could argue for GREY/reservations as Catholic history; my judgment is that the religious centre is art, not faith, worship or the Church's life. Legion of Decency rating not found (Boxoffice and Exhibitor 1965 scans were searched without a hit); it would not change a scope decision. No viewing.

No transcript or subtitle file was found (springfieldspringfield 404; subtitlecat, Subdl (403), YIFY and OpenSubtitles (401) had nothing usable), so the ending rests on Variety ('turns to God on the eve of hanging') and The Exhibitor ('is hung'); whether last sacraments are shown is unverified, so the prose says only that he dies reconciled to God. The archive page numbers are leaf indices from the full-text search ('page n19', 'page n60'); check the links land on the review page. Missouri Encyclopedia gives the premiere as 11 May 1948; AFI's general release date is 19 June 1948. The old record had originalTitle 'The Fighting Father Dunne'; AFI and the Legion list use 'Fighting Father Dunne', so that is now the original title and 'The Fighting Father Dunne' an alternate. Not watched.

tree-of-life.notes: Scope ruling, not quality: the film is widely admired and some Catholic writers (Barron, America) praise its theology of grace. But the family's denomination is never made the subject: Collins calls them ostensibly Catholic; a Dominican Sisters' review (search snippet only) guessed the preaching minister was Episcopal; Malick's own background is Episcopalian (not verified this session). Catholic worship and sacraments are at most incidental colour, which the inclusion bar excludes. Procedural note for the editor: GREY_SPEC says a not-Catholic-centred film should stay HOLD, while HOLD_BRIEF (more recent) says REJECT and reserves HOLD for films whose identity cannot be established. I followed HOLD_BRIEF. Greydanus's Decent Films review could not be located (guessed URL returned 404). The Cannes PDF was read by text extraction (pages 1–5).

quo-vadis-2001.notes: Not in inventory (the 1951 'quo-vadis' is a separate record). Rosenbaum (gore) and Wprost (bloodless lions) disagree: probably different cuts, or Wprost describes the deaths of Christians and Rosenbaum the severed limbs; recorded both. The 2001 coda is the open point: Chrostowski and Wprost confirm St Peter in contemporary Rome; no source describes whether it shows St Peter's Square, the Pope or a modern Mass. A Polish scholarly article (czasopisma.ispan.pl, Kwartalnik Filmowy) apparently discusses the final scene but the host was unreachable. A 1985 Italian miniseries and a longer TV version of this film exist; not checked. SUBS REVIEW 2 (English orig.srt, machine-quality translation): the coda is wordless. Last dialogue "Where are you going, Lord?" (02:10:18) and "We return to Rome" (02:10:48); end titles at 02:11:06. Caveat: this file runs 2h11m against a reported 160 minutes, so it may be a shorter cut, or the coda may run longer in other versions; the visual content of the coda (St Peter's Square? the Pope?) is still not described. Per the editor precedent, even a papal image in a wordless coda would be a reservation, not REJECT. Recommended status unchanged: GREY (reservations), now mainly for nudity.

the-cardinal.notes: Legion A-III from four Exhibitor Legion tables (1963–64). The Americanism link to Leo XIII (Testem benevolentiae, 1899) is my editorial gloss, not a reviewer's; the editor may cut it. Released during Vatican II but depicts 1917–39, so rule (b) does not apply. Not watched. SUBS REVIEW 2 (English orig.srt): closing speech quoted in sources. "Liberty and exaltation of our church" echoes the traditional prayer for the exaltation of Holy Mother Church; "freedoms political as well as religious" is set against totalitarianism, not presented as a doctrine of religious liberty. New item: the salvation-of-non-Catholics answer at 00:27:41, left unqualified (no invincible ignorance) and the follow-up deferred; it states something close to the teaching of Pius IX and the Holy Office's 1949 letter but loosely, so a reservation, not the REJECT precedent (the "invisible Church of goodwill" kind). The brief's "interracial marriage" is not in the film's dialogue: the Georgia episode is school segregation and arson. Status unchanged: GREY (reservations).
